extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, dramatists, literary critics, and students of poetics/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for composing and judging poetic and dramatic works (especially tragedy and epic): what makes a good tragedy/epic, the parts of tragedy, unity, length, character, language, music, spectacle, and the moral/effectual aims of poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as an Art with Knowable Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an art (not mere fancy) with a certain end and therefore certain rules; Aristotle's rules are knowable, grounded in reason and the common sentiment of mankind, and have authority because they conform to nature and produce consistent effects across ages and peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetic composition as a craft guided by principles derived from observation of human passions and the examples of the ancients. Rules are not arbitrary laws but are justified by reason and experience; they should be learned and followed rather than casually rejected as mere constraints. The translator-commentator insists on a literal reading of Aristotle and on explaining obscurities by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: End / Aim of Tragedy (Catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of an action which, by means of pity (compassion) and fear, effects the purification (purging) of such passions; its purpose is morally corrective and instructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose tragedies to arouse pity and fear in order to refine, moderate, and correct the audience's passions — e.g., to restrain ambition, curb anger, or awaken religious feeling. Avoid works that merely titillate curiosity without moral effect. The emotional effect is essential: the play must move the spectator toward a proper mediocrity of passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (Mythos / Fable) — Primacy and Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (fable, mythos) is the chief element of tragedy: it must be a complete and whole action with a beginning, middle and end, exhibiting a necessary and probable sequence (cause-and-effect) that produces pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a unified plot where incidents follow by necessity or probability; include elements like complication and unraveling (peripeteia, anagnorisis) so the sequence logically leads to the tragic outcome. Ensure the action is intelligible as one whole rather than a string of loosely connected episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Strict Unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action imitated must form a single, cohesive whole — the unity of the action is stricter and more perfect in tragedy than in epic because each part in tragedy is a small, interdependent portion of the one whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing multiple, fully independent actions within one tragedy. Each episode should be so connected that taken alone it cannot constitute a complete action; this interdependence strengthens unity and increases dramatic force. Transplanting or padding the action with many self-sufficient episodes weakens unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Appropriate Length (Magnitude and Compactness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should have a proper magnitude — neither too short nor too diffuse; beauty consists in order and magnitude, and compactness is generally more affecting than diffusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a concentrated structure that attains its end in a suitably short span (traditionally a single course of the sun). Excessive extension (epic-like length) dulls the effect; conversely, excessive brevity can make the work seem maimed. Keep the work as compact as the nature of the imitation requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) — Suitability and Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be appropriate to the action: they should be morally credible (generally good or noble in some respect), consistent, and such that their choices and errors (hamartia) plausibly produce the plot's events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose moral status and temperament suit the action; tragic downfall should come from error or frailty rather than from sheer vice (so the audience can pity and fear). Maintain psychological consistency and 'likeness to life' so character actions support the plot's logical sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / Cause of Misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic misfortune should arise from an error or frailty (not from vice alone), so that the hero's fall elicits pity and fear rather than mere condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the protagonist's mistake or ignorance so that readers/spectators understand how it leads to catastrophe and can sympathize. Avoid making misfortune purely the result of moral depravity if the aim is purification by pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — What is Said
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought covers the themes, arguments, and the reasoning expressed in speeches — the intellectual content that supports the action and reveals purpose or insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure speeches and argumentative moments are appropriate to the character and situation and contribute to the demonstration of the action's intelligibility and moral point. The play should present reasoning that helps the audience perceive causes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, style, metaphors, and versification — diction must be apt, clear, and expressive, suiting the characters and contributing to the work's beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select language and metrical patterns appropriate to the genre (iambic for tragedy in Greek practice, hexameter for epic where applicable), employ apt metaphors and figure of speech, and preserve clarity so that the action's import is felt both in reading and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song / Chorus (Melos) as an Integral Part
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus (song and dance) is a constituent part of tragedy and should form a coherent part of the whole, contributing to verisimilitude and the emotional effect; it is not merely an interlude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate chorus material so that its music, lyric, and movement amplify and comment upon the action — it must cohere with the plot rather than appear as an unrelated spectacle. Restoring the chorus strengthens the imitation and the instructive power of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) — Effect but Secondary
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (scenic show, visual display) increases pleasure and sensibility but is the least artistic element in tragedy — it depends more on stagecraft than poetic construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spectacle judiciously: it can heighten immediate effect but must not substitute for a well-constructed plot or sound characterization. Avoid relying on sensational external features that mask weakness in the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable (Fiction) vs History — Universality over Particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable (invented story) is superior to history for poetic instruction because fable speaks to universal truths and general human types, whereas history is particular and less instructive about what 'ought' to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructed incidents that illustrate universal human actions and consequences (fable) rather than mere reporting of events (history) when the aim is moral instruction and emotional purification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation / Mimesis — Representing Actions and Passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry imitates human actions and passions; the rules of poetics derive from this imitation and from how passions operate in humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representations that faithfully present the passions and actions so that the audience recognizes, feels, and learns from them. Rules should be drawn from observation of human nature and its passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate Means (Tragedy vs Epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic genres have different proper means: epic is narrative, extended, and invokes curiosity/admiration; tragedy is represented, compact, uses music/chorus, and aims at pity/fear. Each genre must employ the devices fitting its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not graft epic devices onto tragedy or vice versa without paying heed to how they alter unity and effect. For instance, tragedy's representation and chorus make it suitable for the many; epic's length and episodic range suit other aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (Single Course) and Concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy traditionally confines itself to a single course of the sun (one day) or a compressed time-frame so as to achieve a concentrated imitation of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the temporal scope of a tragedy to maintain intensity and immediacy. If a poetic work expands temporal scope beyond what its genre requires, it risks diluting the dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Corrupt/False Tragedy (Anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: False or corrupted tragic forms focus on particular intrigues, curiosity, and vain unravelings without purifying passions; such works often aim merely to amuse and satisfy curiosity, not to instruct or moderate passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject plays that prioritize clever plotting for curiosity's sake, trivial intrigues, or sensational twists that have no moral or cathartic function. A true tragedy should be educational and corrective, not mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and Necessity — Probable and Necessary Sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The incidents of a poem should follow from one another either by necessity or probability; the ordered arrangement is essential to producing the desired emotional and intellectual effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange episodes so that each follows logically from previous events; contrivances that break causal plausibility weaken the work. The audience's recognition of necessity/probability in events is central to eliciting pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Accessibility — Pleasing Both Sense and Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A work should give pleasure that can be recognized by both ignorant (sensory) and learned (rational) audiences — some elements are judged by sense, others by reason; the best works satisfy both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include elements that immediately please the senses (melody, spectacle in moderation) while also conforming to reasoned rules (unity, probability). Strive for works that unite popular appeal and philosophical soundness so that rules and pleasure are not opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Critical Method and Commentary (Meta-criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation of rules requires philosophical method and examples; commentators should explain rules by reference to the ancient poets (the exemplars) and show obscurities by example rather than idle contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or critiquing poetic works, rely on clear, example-driven exposition grounded in the practice of exemplary poems. Literal translation and careful elucidation of original claims make the rules usable for practitioners.
